content: Many women prefer to avoid pharmacological or invasive methods for managing pain during labor, which has led to the growing popularity of complementary approaches such as acupuncture and acupressure. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of these methods for pain management during labor. It is an update of a previous review published in 2011. To gather evidence, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, MEDLINE, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to February 2019. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared acupuncture or acupressure with placebo, no treatment, or other non-pharmacological pain management methods. Both nulliparous and multiparous women in spontaneous or induced labor were included. Trials using quasi-RCT or cross-over designs were excluded. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 28 trials involving 3960 women. Thirteen trials focused on acupuncture, while 15 examined acupressure. None of the studies were free from bias across all domains. Pain intensity was typically measured using a visual analogue scale (VAS), where lower scores indicated less pain. Acupuncture versus Sham Acupuncture Acupuncture may have little to no effect on the intensity of pain compared to sham acupuncture (mean difference [MD] -4.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] -12.94 to 4.09; 2 trials, 325 women; low-certainty evidence). Acupuncture may increase satisfaction with pain relief compared to sham acupuncture (risk ratio [RR] 2.38, 95% CI 1.78 to 3.19; 1 trial, 150 women; moderate-certainty evidence). Acupuncture probably reduces the use of pharmacological analgesia (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.89; 2 trials, 261 women; moderate-certainty evidence). Acupuncture may have no effect on assisted vaginal birth (very low-certainty evidence) and probably has little to no effect on caesarean section rates (low-certainty evidence). Acupuncture versus Usual Care The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupuncture reduces pain intensity compared to usual care (standardized mean difference [SMD] -1.31, 95% CI -2.14 to -0.49; 4 trials, 495 women; very low-certainty evidence). Acupuncture may have little to no effect on satisfaction with pain relief (low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupuncture reduces the use of pharmacological analgesia (average RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.85; 6 trials, 1059 women; very low-certainty evidence). Acupuncture probably has little to no effect on assisted vaginal birth (low-certainty evidence) or caesarean section rates (low-certainty evidence). Acupuncture versus No Treatment One trial compared acupuncture to no treatment. The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupuncture reduces pain intensity (MD -1.16, 95% CI -1.51 to -0.81; 163 women; very low-certainty evidence), assisted vaginal birth, or caesarean section rates. Acupuncture versus Sterile Water Injection The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupuncture affects the use of pharmacological analgesia, assisted vaginal birth, or caesarean section rates. Acupressure versus Sham Control The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupressure reduces pain intensity during labor (MD -1.93, 95% CI -3.31 to -0.55; 6 trials, 472 women) or affects assisted vaginal birth rates. Acupressure may have little to no effect on the use of pharmacological analgesia (low-certainty evidence). Acupressure probably reduces the caesarean section rate (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.71; 4 trials, 313 women; moderate-certainty evidence). Acupressure versus Usual Care The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupressure reduces pain intensity during labor (SMD -1.07, 95% CI -1.45 to -0.69; 8 trials, 620 women) or increases satisfaction with pain relief (MD 1.05, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.35; 1 trial, 105 women). Acupressure may have little to no effect on caesarean section rates (low-certainty evidence). Acupressure versus Combined Control Acupressure probably slightly reduces pain intensity during labor compared to a combined control (SMD -0.42, 95% CI -0.65 to -0.18; 2 trials, 322 women; moderate-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about whether acupressure affects the use of pharmacological analgesia (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.25; 1 trial, 212 women), satisfaction with childbirth, assisted vaginal birth, or caesarean section rates. Additional Findings No studies reported on the sense of control during labor, and only one study reported on satisfaction with the childbirth experience. Authors' Conclusions Acupuncture, when compared to sham acupuncture, may increase satisfaction with pain management and reduce the use of pharmacological analgesia. Acupressure, when compared to a combined control or usual care, may reduce pain intensity. For other comparisons, the effects of acupuncture and acupressure on pain intensity and satisfaction with pain relief remain uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Acupuncture may have little to no effect on caesarean or assisted vaginal birth rates. Acupressure probably reduces the need for caesarean section when compared to sham control. Further high-quality research is needed, particularly studies that include sham controls, comparisons to usual care, and outcomes such as sense of control during labor, satisfaction with childbirth, and satisfaction with pain relief.
